transcript.text:
A fridge-freezer that isn't keeping cold usually comes down to one of a few things, roughly in this order: 1. Something simple letting warm air in or keeping cold air out: a setting or eco/holiday mode, food pressed against the vents, or a door seal not closing flat.
2. On a frost-free model, an airflow problem: the freezer coil makes the cold for both sections and a fan blows it into the fridge. If the defrost system fails, ice builds up over that coil and chokes the air, or the fan itself can stop. The classic sign is a warm fridge but a still-cold freezer.
3. The coils at the back or underneath clogged with dust, or the unit pushed tight against the wall, so it can't get rid of heat.
4. Less often, the compressor not starting at all, which usually leaves both sections warm. The most useful thing to know first: is the freezer still properly cold while the fridge is warm, and is there a thick layer of ice or snow on the back wall inside the freezer? A cold freezer with a warm fridge points strongly at airflow or defrost; both warm points more towards the compressor side. While you check that, these are quick and safe: 1. Settings: the fridge should be about 3–5°C and the freezer around -18°C, with no eco or holiday mode on. If something was wrong, correct it and give it a day.
2. Vents and loading: cold air usually comes in through vents on the back wall inside the fridge. Move anything pressed against them and loosen tightly packed shelves. Blocked vents alone can make a fridge go warm.
3. Door seals: run your fingers round each rubber seal, looking for splits, gaps or a folded section. A poor seal lets warm air in all the time.
4. Coils at the back: unplug it, gently vacuum the coil or grille at the back or underneath, and leave a few centimetres of space from the wall. If it was very dusty, that may be the whole story, especially if it seems to run constantly. One more thing: if it has just been moved or delivered, it may not be faulty at all. If it was laid on its side, let it stand upright for about 24 hours before switching on. If it was moved upright, wait 2–4 hours, then give it a few hours' running before judging. If food is getting warm, move anything perishable to a cool box or another fridge for now.
[Helpful to see: image "Fridge not cooling — simple checks first" — Before suspecting the sealed system, check the temperature setting, that the door seal closes cleanly, that there's air space and clean condenser coils at the back, and listen for the compressor. Unplug before cleaning at the back. A sealed-system or refrigerant repair is a job for a qualified engineer. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
freezer still cold, fridge warm. milk going off. lots of frost on back wall of freezer

That pattern is very telling. A cold freezer, a warm fridge and heavy frost on the freezer's back wall points strongly at an airflow problem caused by ice. On a frost-free fridge-freezer, one coil behind that freezer back panel makes the cold for both sections, and a fan blows some of it up into the fridge. The defrost system normally melts the frost off that coil every so often. If part of it fails, the frost never clears and slowly builds into a block that chokes the air. The freezer stays cold because it's right next to the coil, but the fridge starves. In order of likelihood:
1. A defrost fault: the defrost heater, the defrost thermostat or the defrost timer/control. This is the most common cause with this much frost.
2. The evaporator fan not running, either failed or jammed by the ice.
3. Less likely, warm damp air getting in past the freezer door seal and adding to the frost. That frost tends to be heaviest near the door rather than spread over the back wall. These checks will help separate them:
1. Fan test: open the freezer and press the door-light/door switch in by hand. If you hear the fan whirr, the fan has power and ice is the likely culprit (defrost). If it's silent, the fan may be dead or frozen in place.
2. Vent test: with both doors shut for a few minutes, open the fridge and feel the vent on the back wall, usually near the top. If the fan is running but little or no cold air is coming through, that's iced-up coils.
3. Manual defrost: this is the real test, and it also gets you going again. Unplug it, move the food into cool bags or another fridge, put towels down and leave the freezer door open until every bit of ice has melted. That usually takes 24–48 hours. Don't chip at the ice or use heat guns. Dry it, plug back in, and give it a day. If the fridge comes back cold after the defrost, that suggests the problem is ice. Watch it closely, though. If the frost builds back up and the fridge goes warm again within a few days to a couple of weeks, one of the defrost parts has failed, and the defrost only bought you time. If the fridge stays warm even with the ice gone, the fan becomes the main suspect. Testing the defrost parts usually means taking the freezer's back panel off. Some owners do that, but many prefer an engineer at that point. Start with the fan and vent tests, and tell me what you hear and feel.
vents at the back of fridge, hardly any cold air coming out. freezer has a faint scraping/ticking noise sometimes, no proper whirr that I could tell

That fits the ice theory well. Hardly any air at the fridge vent, heavy frost on the freezer back wall, and a faint scraping or ticking instead of a steady whirr usually means the fan blade is catching on ice that has built up round it. A fan motor that has simply died tends to be silent or give a steady hum, not a scrape. So my best guess, with moderate confidence, is a defrost system fault: most likely the defrost heater, the defrost thermostat or the defrost timer/control. The second possibility is a fan motor that's struggling or seizing in its own right. The full manual defrost I described last time is now the right next step. It clears the ice and tells the two causes apart:
1. Once every bit of ice has gone and it's dried out, plug it back in. After a few minutes, press the freezer door switch and listen. A clean, steady whirr with no scraping means the fan is fine, and ice was the problem.
2. Give it a day with the doors shut, then feel the fridge vent and check the fridge is cold. If cold air is flowing and the fridge is back to normal, that suggests the defrost system as the cause.
3. Keep an eye on the freezer back wall over the next few days to two weeks. If the frost builds up again and the scraping comes back, one of the defrost parts has failed. The defrost will only have bought you time.
4. If the fan is still silent or still scrapes even with all the ice gone, the evaporator fan motor becomes the main suspect. Until that's done, I'd treat the defrost heater, thermostat or timer as the likely culprit rather than a confirmed one, so don't buy anything yet. Testing or replacing those parts usually means taking the freezer's back panel off. Many owners hand over to an engineer at that point, especially on a newer or frost-free model with an electronic control. Keep the milk and other perishables somewhere cold while it defrosts, and tell me what you hear and feel afterwards.
ok will try the full defrost, got a cool box. no burning smell or tripping btw. how long do I leave it off?

Plan on at least 24 hours switched off, and up to 48 if the frost was really thick. The visible ice on the back wall may melt in a few hours, but the real problem is the ice packed round the coil behind that panel, which you can't see and which melts last. If you switch back on too early, that hidden block stays and you'll be back where you started in a day or two. To make it go smoothly:
1. Unplug it, leave both doors wide open, and put towels on the floor and in the bottom of each section. Change them as they soak up meltwater.
2. To speed it up safely, put a bowl or two of hot (not boiling) water in the freezer and close the door for 15–20 minutes at a time, then reopen. Don't chip at the ice, and don't use a hairdryer or heat gun.
3. Once you can see no ice at all, leave it a few more hours with the doors open. The best sign it's done is water no longer dripping from behind the back panel.
4. Look for the small drain hole at the bottom of the back wall. If it seems blocked, flush it gently with warm water from a squeezy bottle or baster. A blocked drain can add to ice build-up.
5. Dry everything, plug back in, and leave the doors shut. Keep the food in the cool box until the freezer is properly cold again, which usually takes a few hours. The fridge can take most of a day. No burning smell and no tripping is reassuring. It points away from an electrical fault and fits the ice explanation. Once it's back on, press the freezer door switch and listen for a clean, steady whirr, and check the fridge vent is blowing cold the next day. Let me know what you find. The key thing then is whether the frost starts building up again over the following days, as that would confirm a defrost part has failed.

Settings, blocked vents/over-packing or door seal letting warm air in (medium)
Dusty condenser coils / poor ventilation round the unit (low)
Compressor or its start relay not running (both sections warm) (low)
